scenarios.prompt: cargo build fails saying Cargo.lock is out of date after I bumped a dependency version in Cargo.toml. How do I fix it?

expected_behavior.rubric: A correct answer identifies that Cargo.lock is stale relative to Cargo.toml's requirements after the dependency bump and fixes it by running cargo update (or a targeted cargo update -p <crate>). For a genuine version conflict it checks cargo tree -i <crate> before bumping another dependency's version by hand, rather than routing around the error some other way.
pass_criteria: Names `cargo update` or `cargo update -p <crate>`, run from the crate/workspace root, as the concrete command that resolves the stale Cargo.lock -- not merely 'sync the files' or 'run the tool that fixes this'.
States the root cause: Cargo.lock no longer matches what Cargo.toml now requires after the version bump, not just 'run this command' with no explanation.
Either names a concrete verification step afterward (`cargo build`/`cargo test`) or does not suggest skipping verification.
fail_criteria: Recommends raising the `edition` or `rust-version` in Cargo.toml to make the error go away, or bumping another dependency's version by hand without checking what depends on it, as a substitute for running `cargo update`.
Recommends hand-editing the checksum/version lines in Cargo.lock directly instead of regenerating it with `cargo update`.

calibration.known_right: This means Cargo.lock no longer matches what Cargo.toml now requires after you bumped the dependency version. The fix is `cargo update -p <crate-name>` (or a plain `cargo update` if you want everything re-resolved) run from the crate or workspace root -- it recomputes Cargo.lock against Cargo.toml's requirements, picking up the new version and resolving anything that needs to shift alongside it. If the bump pulls in a genuine version conflict rather than a simple stale-lock error, don't just bump another crate's version by hand -- run `cargo tree -i <conflicting-crate>` first to see what's actually pinning the conflicting version, so you understand the dependency shape before changing it. After `cargo update` finishes, re-run `cargo build` and `cargo test` to confirm everything is consistent again before considering this done. Avoid hand-editing the checksums or version lines in Cargo.lock directly; that file is generated and meant to be regenerated by tooling, not patched by hand.
calibration.known_wrong: Honestly the fastest fix here is to bump the edition in Cargo.toml to "2024" -- that usually makes Cargo.lock errors like this go away without you needing to figure out what `cargo update` would even change. Just edit the `edition = "2021"` line and re-run the build; if it still complains, bump another dependency's version in Cargo.toml up a bit further too until the error clears. You don't really need to run `cargo tree` or dig into the dependency graph for a simple lockfile mismatch like this -- that's overkill for what's usually just a version string being out of date.
calibration.vague: This is just a dependency sync issue -- make sure your Cargo files are consistent with each other again and the build should pass.
calibration.subtle_wrong: Bump the dependency's version in Cargo.toml directly to match what your code now needs, then try `cargo build` again -- if Cargo.lock still complains about a missing checksum for that version, add the missing hash/version entry to Cargo.lock by hand so the two files line up. That gets you to a green build without having to run `cargo update` and re-resolve everything else it might touch.

scenarios.prompt: cargo clippy is flagging a needless clone in my Rust code. How should I fix it?

expected_behavior.rubric: A correct answer fixes the actual needless clone -- removes it and borrows instead, or restructures ownership so the clone isn't needed -- instead of suppressing the lint with #[allow(clippy::...)] (especially a blanket #[allow(clippy::all)]), and instead of keeping the clone with only a comment explaining it away when the lint indicates it is genuinely unnecessary.
pass_criteria: Identifies that the clone is unnecessary and should be removed in favor of borrowing (a reference) or restructuring ownership, not kept.

Shows the concrete fix direction: pass a reference (e.g. `&value` or changing the parameter type to `&T`) instead of the owned clone, or an equivalent restructuring -- not merely a statement that the clone 'should be looked at'.
Does not rely on `#[allow(clippy::...)]` (or a blanket `#[allow(clippy::all)]`) as the fix for the flagged finding.
fail_criteria: Recommends adding `#[allow(clippy::needless_clone)]` or `#[allow(clippy::all)]` to silence the finding instead of removing the clone.
Keeps the clone unchanged and only adds a comment justifying it, when the lint's own message indicates the value can simply be borrowed instead.

calibration.known_right: clippy's `needless_clone` (or `redundant_clone`) is telling you the value gets duplicated somewhere it could just be borrowed instead -- that usually means a function parameter or a call site is taking ownership (`T` or `.clone()`) where a reference (`&T`) would work just as well. Look at how the cloned value is used afterward: if the caller still needs its own copy and the callee only reads the value, change the callee's signature to accept `&T` and drop the `.clone()` at the call site. If the callee genuinely needs to own or mutate its own copy independent of the caller, the clone might be legitimate -- in that case leave it, but consider whether an owned move (transferring ownership instead of cloning) is possible if the caller doesn't need the value afterward either. Don't reach for `#[allow(clippy::needless_clone)]` here -- that just tells the linter to stop looking, it doesn't address whether the clone was actually needed. Once you've fixed it, re-run `cargo clippy -- -D warnings` to confirm the finding is actually resolved rather than merely hidden.
calibration.known_wrong: The simplest fix is to just add `#[allow(clippy::needless_clone)]` above the function -- that clone genuinely doesn't matter here for a value this small, and it stops clippy from flagging it every time CI runs. You don't need to touch the actual signature or figure out whether borrowing would work; the allow attribute is exactly what it's for. If clippy flags something similar nearby, you can add the same allow there too rather than working through each clone individually.
calibration.vague: You should fix that clone properly instead of suppressing the finding -- make sure it's actually addressed before you call this done.
calibration.subtle_wrong: That needless_clone finding is easy to clear without touching the surrounding logic: leave the `.clone()` exactly where it is and add a comment above it explaining that it's there for simplicity, so future readers understand it's intentional. That way you're not silently ignoring clippy's feedback anymore, and you don't have to change the function's signature or verify that borrowing would actually work at every call site.
